Beyond faster analysis Kübra Sak Artificial Intelligence Product Management Customer Experience Data Analytics Beyond the First Answer: Designing AI for Deeper Understanding Kübra Sak 5 min read · Sep 26, 2026 -- 1 Listen Share What changes when AI helps us move from observations to hypotheses, evidence, and better questions? Generative AI has made it remarkably easy to ask questions of our data. But I think one of its most interesting opportunities begins when the question itself is not obvious. Imagine this: Customer complaints are relatively stable. Yet sales are declining, and more existing customers are leaving. Nothing in the most obvious signal seems dramatic. So what are we missing? Have customer expectations changed while the metrics we monitor have remained the same? Are customers becoming dissatisfied without explicitly complaining? Were the signals already present in conversations, behaviors, or interactions — but fragmented across different sources and therefore difficult to see? Did the experience deteriorate at a point we were not measuring? Or has the market changed while we continued looking at the problem through the same assumptions? There may not be one immediate answer. And that is exactly where I find AI-powered analysis most interesting. The opportunity is not only to answer the question we already know how to ask. It is to help us discover what else we should be asking. The most important signal may not be the most obvious one Traditional analysis often starts with something we already know how to measure. Complaints increased. Sales decreased. Churn increased. A particular KPI changed. Then we investigate why. But complex customer behavior does not always reveal itself through one metric. A customer does not necessarily complain before leaving. A changing expectation may first appear as a subtle shift in language. A friction point may appear across several interactions without ever becoming the primary reason for contact. A competitor, a new behavior, or a changing market expectation may gradually become more relevant before it creates a visible movement in the metrics we normally monitor. The information may already exist. The challenge may be recognizing that separate signals are telling us part of the same story. This is where AI creates a different analytical opportunity. Its ability to work across large amounts of structured and unstructured information can help us discover patterns and relationships that would be difficult to define as a query in advance. For analytical products, this raises an interesting possibility: What if we do not always have to know exactly what we are looking for before we start looking? From observation to understanding Suppose our starting observation is: Sales are declining and customer churn is increasing, while complaint levels remain relatively stable. AI might surface several patterns. Perhaps customers who later leave increasingly mention price-value concerns. Perhaps explicit complaints remain stable, but expressions of uncertainty, comparison, effort, or unmet expectations are becoming more common. Perhaps the change is concentrated in a particular customer group or appears after a certain interaction. Or perhaps the strongest change is not visible in customer conversations at all — which itself becomes useful information. None of these should immediately become the answer . They represent different stages of investigation. I find it useful to think about the process this way: Observation → Pattern → Hypothesis → Evidence → Next Question An observation tells us something changed. A pattern shows us where signals begin to concentrate. A hypothesis gives us a possible explanation. Evidence helps us understand how strongly that explanation is supported and where its boundaries are. And the next question allows us to continue the investigation. AI can potentially support every stage of this journey. One answer can open several directions Imagine AI identifies an increase in price-value concerns among customers who later leave. That is useful. But it becomes much more interesting when it opens new directions. Is price itself the issue, or has the perception of value changed? Do customers with similar prices but different experiences behave differently? Did these customers previously give us signals that we did not recognize as churn indicators? Are expectations changing equally across customer groups? Is the pattern new, or has it existed for months without becoming visible in our traditional metrics? What happened immediately before customer behavior started to change? And perhaps the most uncomfortable but valuable question: Are we investigating the customer with today’s behavior, but yesterday’s assumptions? Now AI is doing more than retrieving information. It is helping create an investigation. Sometimes the data was already telling us Organizations may not always suffer from a lack of data. Sometimes the signal may already be there. It may exist in conversations, behavioral changes, repeated friction, abandoned journeys, changing questions, comparisons, expectations, or patterns across multiple interactions. Individually, none of these signals may look important enough. AI gives us new ways to examine them together. It can help connect information across sources, identify changes in language or behavior, compare groups, surface unusual concentrations, and suggest relationships worth investigating.
